NPR News
An unexpected activist emerged to help block a $5 billion data center in Maryland
WAMU 88.5 |
By
Jenny Abamu
Published November 7, 2026 at 2:00 AM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR
Taylor Frazier McCollum has been active in the opposition to the possible data center at the site of the demolished Landover Mall in Prince George's County, less than a mile from where she lived. If the project is built, the development could occupy more than 80 acres.
The overgrown grass and weeds seem to stretch into the horizon on nearly 90 acres of empty land in Landover, Md. It used to be Landover Mall, but that closed in 2002, and the site has been mostly vacant since.
In 2024, the developer that built the mall won approval from county planners for a $5 billion data center campus, and word began spreading through the largely Black community nearby.
"I was like, 'Oh, hell no,'" said Taylor Frazier McCollum, describing the moment she learned about the project. She lived less than a mile away from it. "Why would you want to bring water-polluting, diesel-generating data centers right down the street from where people live, work, play? It just didn't make sense to me."
Sponsored
Frazier McCollum is one of a number of Americans whose political awakening was triggered by data center development. Across the country, community members have taken to local council hearings to voice their opposition. They've prompted — though estimates vary — about 500 moratoriums on data centers nationwide.
A different kind of land-use activist
Unlike a lot of land-use activists trying to protect their homes from threats in their backyards, Frazier McCollum does not own a home. In 2024, she and her young daughter were evicted from their apartment. She was working at a waxing center that cut wages, and she could no longer cover her rent.
"It was difficult," Frazier McCollum recalled. "Because I created the ideal life paying for us to live in this apartment and have our own space ... and then to have it taken away ... It felt like something that wasn't ever going to end."
They've moved around and were living in her grandfather's home when she learned about the proposed project less than a mile away.
Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR /
Taylor Frazier McCollum in front of her grandfather's home, where she lived when she heard about the proposed data center site less than a mile away in Landover, Md.
She created a petition that gathered over 25,000 signatures, leading to widely attended protests and culminating in multiple local moratoriums imposed on data centers throughout the county. It blocked the $5 billion project that was set to break ground between 2026 and 2027.
The fight pushed Frazier McCollum to the forefront of local politics. She went to county meetings, testified before Maryland legislators and endorsed political candidates. She found herself in a coalition of socialists, environmentalists, people angry about their electric bills and neighbors new to organizing.
Sponsored
Local media interviewed her, and people in data center circles called her "the Landover girl."
After some losses, the county needs revenue, and data centers could help
Staci Hartwell, a longtime local environmental activist, says she spent years struggling to get traction on the data center issue before Frazier McCollum came along.
"This is something that was happening in her neighborhood, and it was really like her awakening," Hartwell said.
But with data centers paused, some in Prince George's County worry about declining tax revenue. Last year, a local Six Flags closed. The NFL's Washington Commanders announced plans to return to neighboring Washington, D.C. Thousands of federal workers have lost their jobs. The county faces a budget deficit.
Tyrone Turner/WAMU for NPR /
The possible data center site, which was once the Landover Mall, in Prince George's County. If the project is built, the development will occupy more than 80 acres.
In September, Frazier McCollum appeared at a county council meeting to advocate for a fund for roof repairs, something her grandfather's home needs. Council member Wanika Fisher, who supports moving some data center projects forward, reminded her that the county needs development.
"Our county has an economic future that we have to grapple with," said Fisher, addressing the request. "I don't see where the money is coming from. I think we have to have a real conversation. And I'm not saying that a data center is the answer, but I'm saying it's worth the hard discussion."
Sponsored
Now Frazier McCollum is broadening her activism and going to new places
With the Landover project on hold, Frazier McCollum now wants a full ban on that and other data center projects. And with grants Hartwell and others have found, Frazier McCollum has taken her message to Black communities fighting data center growth in Atlanta, Memphis and even across the globe in Zambia.
"I feel like so many people are depending on this fight to be successful," Frazier McCollum explained. "Not just for myself, but even across the country, to set precedent for other people that are fighting against hyperscale data centers."
She's lost out on work to attend public meetings or knock on doors, and she's relied on family for rides and childcare.
Her father, Lacy McCollum Jr., sees the data center fight as rooted in civil rights.
"We're talking about the right to water, the right to clean air, the right to a place to live. That's everybody's fight,

Take heart, Seattle. Soup season is upon us
KUOW |
By
Brandi Fullwood
Published November 6, 2026 at 4:57 PM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
Brandi Fullwood
KUOW
A glorious, heart warming bowl of mi thap cam at Thọ Tường in South Lake Union.
As the incoming days of rain threaten to push us inside, Seattle restaurants are breaking out the big bowls and filling them up with all kinds of chowders, stews, and medleys to warm and nourish you.
But which ones are worth leaving your house for? On a recent episode of “Seattle Eats,” The Stranger’s Meg van Huygen and I shared some of the best soups — simmered-for-hours, house-made this and that, glossy and glimmering — around the city.
Animal Ramen at Pidgin Cooperative in Interbay / Fishermen's Terminal for $24
Sponsored
The hype machine is right. Pidgin Cooperative is a delightful place to steam your face with a big bowl of ramen with all the fix-ins.
The Animal Ramen, the non-vegetarian option, “has lots of little treasures that you can mine for.”
It's interactive,” van Huygen said.
Nestled artfully inside of the bowl are a whole host of house-made ingredients: thin, chewy noodles, pork belly, char siu, an onsen egg — slow poached until silky and custardy. There are seasonal veggies like leeks, slivered purple daikon, maybe zucchini.
All the gold that glimmers in the Animal Ramen is in Pidgin’s distractingly good broth. Unctuous, rich, with a satin-full-bodied finish. Soup-nosis ensues and it’s hard to remember to do anything else but sip and slurp.
“People may look at a bowl of ramen and see it as simple,” Sean Case, a cook at Pidgin Cooperative, said. “But hours go into making just the broth.”
Brandi Fullwood
A bowl of ramen with plenty of little treasures and a distractingly good broth at Pidgin Cooperative in Interbay
Pidgin focuses on layering flavors to make it special, not just over hours, but days. Case and fellow cooks start by simmering chicken bones and chicken feet, and dried anchovy; straining the fat and then adding it back later.
Sponsored
The broth is largely unseasoned except for gyofun, a Japanese fish powder, as well as 1 ounce of pork and chicken fat.
Case is newer to the team but he said the process of making the broth alone has deepened his appreciation for the business.
Pidgin Cooperative is not just a name but a model for the business. The whole staff is invited to be co-owners in the cooperative structure.
After a year or so, full-time workers can buy a membership share and that allows them to vote, see finances, and get a slice of the profits
“It takes a village to run a restaurant perhaps,” van Huygen said.
She wrote about the Pidgin Cooperative in a feature for The Stranger, earlier this year.
“They're so thoughtful because they really know their ingredients,” she said. “They're all incredibly fresh because they're local producers.”
Sponsored
Zachary Pacleb, chef and a member owner of Pidgin, van Huygen shared, knows exactly what is in season thanks to a spreadsheet he uses to track when farmers and purveyors will have, for instance, the sweetest asparagus on hand.
“It's very smart,” she said. “He's very organized about his vegetables.”
We agree on this soup and all of its delightful bits and we largely agree on soup season.
“You can eat soup any time of the year. You can eat soup when it's 100 degrees outside. However, I hate it when it's 100 degrees outside,” she said. “The summer was long on the tooth and I just did not wanna eat soup.”
And that’s where I draw the line.
Disclaimer: I don’t actually believe in soup season. I believe that soup for all its effort and glory should be eaten year-round. And thankfully, at many restaurants around the city, there are plenty served on the daily.
Take for instance, the line-worthy pork bone broth soups served at Busan Jeong on Capitol Hill.
Sponsored
Soondaeguk at Busan Jeong on Capitol Hill for $21.95
After opening in March, it is clear that there is no season for this soup. Spring, summer, and fall diners alike wait 40 minutes for a chance to tuck into a quintessential Korean cuisine comfort meal. Busan Jeong makes soups for Juneuary, for "Soup Season," and whenever it's right now.
After waiting my turn, I ordered the effortfully made Soondaeguk, which comes with various sides and sauces — kimchi, chives, and vinegar.
“In Korea, soondaeguk is a very everyday kind of meal. People eat it after work, with friends, alone, or even the morning after drinking. It’s a food that quietly welcomes everybody,” owner Hoyeon Park shares over email.
He said that growing up in Busan, Korea, he ate soondaeguk late nights with his family but as an adult he reaches for it in all kinds of scenarios, “when I’m tired, stressed, or just need something comforting.”
“Soondaeguk has always felt like more than just food to me,” he said. “It’s the kind of meal that makes you feel like you’re home again.”
When soondaeguk arrives at the table, you are served a hot stone pot of pork bone broth that has simmered until the broth turns into a milky white color (several hours), tender slices of pork belly, and of course soondae–blood sausage. At Busan Jeong the blood sausage is made in house — lush and plump, packed full of chives, and glass noodles.
Sponsored
“For first-time guests
, I usually recommend tasting the broth as it is for the first few bites,” Park said. “After that, they can slowly adjust it.”
“We think part of the experience is finding your own perfect bowl,” he said.
Brandi Fullwood
You can customize the line-worthy pork bone broth

Bellevue court offers alternatives to jail while still holding defendants accountable
KUOW |
By
Ruby de Luna
Published November 6, 2026 at 4:17 PM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
Ruby de Luna
KUOW
A sign in the Bellevue Library directs visitors to Bellevue Community Court.
Every Thursday afternoon, community court is in session at Bellevue Library. There is no courtroom. The judge doesn’t wear a robe, or sit on a high bench. Instead, proceedings take place in a conference room, around a horseshoe shaped table. The informal setting is intentional.
Launched last year, Bellevue Community Court is an alternative court for defendants involved in nonviolent, non-serious criminal cases. It is a collaboration between King County District Court, the city of Bellevue, and Bellevue Library.
“We found that there are so many defendants who are accused of things like theft or trespass who have underlying addiction issues,” said Presiding Judge Lisa O’Toole.
Sponsored
When those underlying issues aren’t addressed, many end up cycling through the system.
Community Court is an alternative to traditional court with a focus on treatment, community service, and resources to help participants.
“Community Court individually devises a program for each person, to give them the resources and the tools they need to make changes in their lives,” O’Toole said.
Often, participants don’t need to go far to seek help. Outside the conference room, tables are set up where participants can meet with a team that helps them sign up for substance-abuse treatment, housing assistance, and other resources.
“Community Court is an alternative to incarceration,” said Craig Fritz, probation manager for the city of Bellevue. “It’s also, in a way, an alternative to probation.”
In a traditional court, a defendant appears before a judge for sentencing, Fritz said. If they’re doing well with compliance, that’s the last time they see the judge. But in Community Court, participants are required to perform community service and have a weekly court check-in.
“They’re able to talk to the judge and give them updates,” Fritz said. They tell the judge what they’ve accomplished and achieved over the week. Those updates, he said, provide more than accountability.
Sponsored
“Providing that opportunity for them does a lot for boosting their self confidence and their self-esteem, and having a chance to be listened to,” Fritz said.
Between July 2025 to October 2026, 42 defendants opted into the program. Fritz said the completion rate has been 100%, with no subsequent offenses after graduation.
In addition to Bellevue, King County District Court has launched community courts in Redmond and Shoreline-Kenmore.

NPR News
The economy propelled Democrats to victory. What can they actually do about it?
NPR |
By
Barbara Sprunt
Published November 6, 2026 at 1:53 PM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
Win McNamee
Getty Images
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., are seen here on the steps of the U.S. Capitol on May 21, 2026. The pair of Democratic leaders have acknowledged the public wants them to act quickly on issues of affordability with their newfound majority come January.
Updated November 7, 2026 at 2:00 AM PST
After a sweeping set of midterm victories, Congressional Democratic leaders say they're clear-eyed about their mandate come January.
"We're going to fight to make sure that we make this country affordable for every single American," said Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries, who is the presumptive House speaker, on Tuesday night. "This is a change election, and we understand as House Democrats we need to deliver dramatic change."
Sponsored
Speaking to reporters on Wednesday, Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., added "relief is on the way" but acknowledged some of the public may be skeptical that Democrats can deliver on the economic message that catapulted them to recapturing both chambers of Congress.
Democrats will control the legislative branch, but won't have a large enough majority to overturn a presidential veto and will likely face Republican filibusters in the Senate.
"That doesn't mean that nothing can happen, but it means there are real obstacles," said Bobby Kogan, senior director of federal budget policy at the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank based in Washington, D.C.
Matt Bennett of Third Way, a center-left think tank, said those obstacles create the potential for voters to be disappointed by the limitations inherent in divided government.
"What Democrats were really promising was: return us to power, we will put a check on Trump for two years, and then when we get the White House in 2028, we can actually make your lives better. It isn't clear to me that voters heard the entire message," Bennett said. "They might have just heard the last part, and so there is some risk that voters will be disappointed."
The power of playing offense
An important power that comes with being in the majority is controlling which bills make it to the floor for a vote.
Sponsored
"There will be plenty of bills where the purpose is contrast — Democrats are for this and Republicans are against that," Kogan said. "But what is special about controlling both chambers is that legislation where the public is on [Democrats'] side and it's very difficult for Republicans to argue why they're against it, those sorts of things become real."
As an example, he points to the release of the Epstein files. President Trump and Republican leadership worked to prevent the measure from reaching the floor last year. Once it was brought to a vote in the House via a legislative end run around Speaker Mike Johnson, lawmakers were forced to go on the record and voted nearly unanimously to release the files.
"The difficulty was just getting it there," Kogan said. "And what Democrats can do is they can make popular things get there."
Forcing votes on popular issues has been a winning strategy in previous divided governments. After Democrats won control of Congress in the 2006 midterm elections, they made raising the minimum wage a signature issue, and Republican President George W. Bush went on to sign it into law.
Democrats have signaled plans to put forth bills to help Americans with health care costs, bring back enhanced premium tax credits, and undo Medicaid cuts.
"I think that's going to be critically important — that when you vote for a Democrat, your life improves," said Rebecca Cooke, the Wisconsin Democrat who unseated GOP incumbent Derrick Van Orden in the state's 3rd congressional district.
Democrats also have the ability to use budget reconciliation, a tool that bypasses the threat of a Senate filibuster by allowing certain budget-related bills to pass with a simple majority. Democrats used reconciliation to pass some health care changes in 2010. Republicans used it to pass tax cuts in 2017, and it was used to pass Trump's signature tax and spending bill.
Sponsored
Massachusetts Sen. Elizabeth Warren is already calling on her party to embrace reconciliation, writing in Time this week that Democrats should use it to "reverse Republican health care cuts, expand health care coverage, and fund universal child care."
Embrace the veto
Trump has sent mixed signals about what kind of leader he'll be in divided government, saying he'll "veto everything" and that he could "make deals" with Democrats.
Congressional Democrats are already pushing back at the idea that a veto is a deterrent.
"If we have a bill that is bipartisan to restore healthcare for the people who lost their Medicaid or to improve access to affordable medicines and other things, like, I dare him to veto that," Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand told Morning Edition. "If he decides to veto the common sense things that get groceries down or housing prices down, then '28's going to be very favorable for Democrats."
Embracing the veto – rather than running away from it – can be an effective political tool.

MARY LOUISE KELLY, HOST:
At the top of the charts this week is a band that has waited a long time for its first No. 1 album. Stephen Thompson of NPR Music explains.
STEPHEN THOMPSON, BYLINE: This week's Billboard pop charts reflect the seven days just before Halloween, so a few spooky perennials haunt the latest charts. Scan the new Hot 100, and you'll find Michael Jackson's "Thriller," Rockwell's "Somebody's Watching Me," and a signature song from "The Nightmare Before Christmas," "This Is Halloween."
Sponsored
(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "THIS IS HALLOWEEN")
UNIDENTIFIED ACTORS: (As characters, singing) This is Halloween. This is Halloween. Halloween, Halloween, Halloween, Halloween.
THOMPSON: The week's biggest surprise is a milestone performance for a long-running band that knows its way around the darkness. For the first time in a career spanning 25 years, the Gothic pop punk band My Chemical Romance has the No. 1 album in the country.
(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "WELCOME TO THE BLACK PARADE")
MY CHEMICAL ROMANCE: (Singing) Because one day, I'll leave you a phantom to lead you in the summer to join the black parade.
THOMPSON: "The Black Parade" came out in 2006, when it debuted and peaked at No. 2 on the Billboard albums chart. The record remained My Chemical Romance's highest-charting album in the 20 years following its original release. And in honor of "The Black Parade's" 20th anniversary, the band has gone all out to commemorate the album.
(SOUNDBITE OF SONG, "WELCOME TO THE BLACK PARADE")
Sponsored
MY CHEMICAL ROMANCE: (Singing) Your memory will carry on, will carry on.
THOMPSON: My Chemical Romance has been playing songs from "The Black Parade" on tour for months now, and it's just released a deluxe edition of the album with bonus tracks. That reissue includes many different versions on vinyl and CD, which has helped give "The Black Parade" a huge sales boost. "The Black Parade" has now set a new Billboard chart record. The 20-year gap between its debut and its first week at No. 1 has been the longest in chart history. Stephen Thompson, NPR Music.

Black voter turnout helped contribute to major Democratic wins
NPR |
By
Marc Rivers,
Ailsa Chang, Tinbete Ermyas
Published November 6, 2026 at 1:53 PM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
AILSA CHANG, HOST:
The blue tsunami of Democratic victories in the midterms was partly powered by a groundswell of support among Black voters. That's especially true in the South, where many voting rights activists had feared the Supreme Court decision gutting the Voting Rights Act would have weakened Black voting power. To help us make sense of all of this, we have called Andra Gillespie. She's a professor of political science at Emory University in Atlanta. Welcome.
ANDRA GILLESPIE: Thank you.
Sponsored
CHANG: So I know we're just a few days out from the election, and there are still some races that have yet to be called, but overall, how big of an increase in Black voter participation did we see in this election compared to the 2024 election or even previous midterm election cycles, do you think?
GILLESPIE: So I'm going to use my state of Georgia as an example because Georgia does collect data on voter turnout by race. That would be really helpful in this election cycle. So in absolute terms, compared to 2022, we saw higher voter turnout amongst African Americans, Latinos and Asian American voters in the state of Georgia. White voters actually had lower voter turnout compared to 2022. And so that actually helps to contribute to overall Black and Asian American voters in particular making up a larger share of the 2026 electorate than they did amongst registered voters.
CHANG: What about Black male voters? I want to focus on them for a moment because President Trump did make some inroads with Black men back in 2024, even though they still largely voted for Kamala Harris. And now I see that exit polls are showing a swing back to Democrats among Black men. So I'm curious, why do you think this is happening, or what is happening?
GILLESPIE: If I had to proffer a hypothesis...
CHANG: Yeah.
GILLESPIE: ...It's probably because of economic issues. One of the things that's actually really interesting nationally if we look at the voter poll or the exit poll data, the economy ranked as the top issue amongst voters overall, but especially in southern states like South Carolina and Georgia and Mississippi, Black voters were actually more likely to cite the economy as their top issue than we saw in those national averages.
CHANG: I want to talk about the historic nature of this election that maybe transcends party politics. I mean, in the governor races, you see this especially. There were a number of historic firsts. You had David Crowley elected as Wisconsin's first Black governor, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the country's first Black woman governor, Byron Donalds, who was elected to become Florida's first Black governor. And I know that these are all different races. These are distinct individuals I'm talking about. But do you see any through line in the role that Black voters may have played in these particular historic wins?
Sponsored
GILLESPIE: Well, yes, but I think there's also this larger issue of candidates supply and Black politicians feeling confident enough that they can run for statewide office. You know, a generation ago, two generations ago, this would have been a risky move, so if you had a really safe congressional seat, like Congressman Donalds', had you might not choose to run (ph), especially if you were a Democrat for statewide office, because you're going to give up a guaranteed seat in order to take a risk and run for a seat that you might not eventually win.
CHANG: Yeah.
GILLESPIE: Well, there's been more examples of Blacks being able to run successfully for statewide office in both the Democratic and the Republican Parties. And I think Stacey Abrams' work in 2018, though it was unsuccessful in getting her to the governor's mansion, actually proved that Black candidates could be viable.
CHANG: What about the role of redistricting? Because earlier this year, the Supreme Court struck down a key provision of the Voting Rights Act, right? And many Democrats and voting rights activists thought this would weaken Black voting power. Then we saw a number of Southern states move to redraw congressional maps in a way that experts said would further diminish Black representation across all levels of government. But it doesn't look like that happened. Why not, you think?
GILLESPIE: What we saw across the South in North Carolina, in Tennessee, Texas, you see these instances of Republican voting strength being diluted to try to create as many seats as possible. And what it did in a wave or tsunami election year was create these districts that Democrats could actually compete in.
CHANG: Was there anything about this year's elections that gave you any indications about where the Black vote might go going forward after this particular midterm election?
GILLESPIE: Republicans miscalculated in 2024 that those defections towards the Republican Party in that election were evidence of some type of permanent realignment...
Sponsored
CHANG: Right.
GILLESPIE: ...Instead of looking at what factors might have been influencing people to vote. What that means going forward is that neither party should consider this current election as indicative of what's going to happen in future elections.
CHANG: Andra Gillespie, political science professor at Emory University, thank you very much for joining us today.
GILLESPIE: Thank you. Transcript provided by

Seattle's Elliott Bay Book Company celebrates 50 years with Rick Simonson
KUOW |
By
Katie Campbell
Published November 6, 2026 at 1:50 PM PST
Facebook
Twitter
LinkedIn
Email
KUOW Photo/Megan Farmer
Rick Simonson is portrayed on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, at Elliott Bay Book Company in Seattle.
Like the bookstore he's worked in for the last 50 years, Rick Simonson is full of stories.
Some stories are quite recent, like in September, when he ran off to get a book for author Yann Martel's talk at the Seattle edition of the Jaipur Literature Festival.
He struck up a conversation with a woman who'd recently moved here from Southern India. As they talked, Brinda Sarathy, dean of the University of Washington Bothell's School of Interdisciplinary Arts and Sciences, approached.
Sponsored
"The  woman I was talking to was [Brinda's] eighth grade English teacher [in India]," Simonson said, still flabbergasted. "Here's somebody who probably had a hand in... shaping the writer and scholar she would grow up to be. And they're both in Seattle."
Simonson is a deeply humble man. He has a tendency to leave out some of the more spectacular moments in his stories, moments when he helped shape the literary world around him.
"I was glad he brought up Yann Martel," said Tracy Taylor, co-owner of Elliott Bay Book Company, who'd sat down with another bookseller to listen to Simonson talk to KUOW. " We had Yann Martel here for 'Life of Pi,' and 10 people showed up. No one knew the book. The book had just gotten published. No one had heard of Yann Martel. Rick had read an early copy of that, went to the publisher, got them to send Yann Martel out to the Pacific Northwest, and we had 10 people. A year later, we had Yann Martel back in the store for the paperback, and we had to turn people away from that reading. That is who Rick is."
Simonson is also the kind of person who tells the story of how books reunited a student with her long-ago teacher rather than the story of how he very likely introduced a great author to the region.
He's been doing both — building community in Seattle and hobnobbing with literary luminaries all over the world — for 50 years now. Elliott Bay Book Company invited readers to celebrate Simonson on Nov. 7, though not everyone could wait until Saturday.
" Rick and I have walked many trails together. But Rick is always too modest, and he always deflects," said Simonson's best friend and a legendary bookseller himself, Paul Yamazaki. As Yamazaki talked about his friend's modesty, Simonson turned away before he cut in, "He does it, though! He does it! He got tagged with an award he couldn't get out of!" (Yamazaki received the National Book Foundation's 2023 Literarian Award for Outstanding Service to the American Literary Community.)
Yamazaki, principal buyer at City Lights Booksellers and Publishers in San Francisco, said they met "through conversation, through serendipity, and we found ourselves knocking at the same doors."
Sponsored
KUOW Photo/Megan Farmer
Paul Yamazaki, left, and Rick Simonson, right, laugh together while being portrayed on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026, at Elliott Bay Book Company in Seattle.
It was easy to see how serendipity led to a decades-long friendship. Talking to the pair is a lot like reading a good book — they tell stories that sweep the literary world with characters like English novelist John Berger and Sonny Mehta, editor-in-chief of the publishing giant Alfred A. Knopf. But they don't just tell a linear story, no, not these two. They both suffer from a kind of ultra-modest syndrome. As one talks, the other is laughing in embarrassment (Yamazaki) or turning away from the conversation and shaking his head, trying to politely find an opportunity to turn the topic around (Simonson).
They've been everywhere together, yucking it up on the streets of Chicago in the middle of the night (Tracy Taylor heard them a block over) and marveling over the luxury of the original Jaipur Literature Festival.
" I've stood at the bottom of a stairway in Jaipur, in India, and all of a sudden... everything goes quiet," Yamazaki said. "And somebody says, 'Oh, Rick is here.'"
How Simonson got here exactly is, of course, another story, one that shows just how deeply ingrained he is in the fabric of Elliott Bay.
He'd been working at a restaurant around the corner from the shop's original location in Pioneer Square, and in 1976, founder Walter Carr offered him a job — in construction.
And so, Simonson started working on one of Elliott Bay's first expansions, "hauling sheet rock and cutting up two-by-fours and sweeping up sawdust and prying things apart," along with his coworker from the restaurant, now also a prominent bookseller, Peter Miller. Miller owns Peter Miller Architecture and Design Books and has written several books, including this month's KUOW Book Club pick, "Lunch at the Shop," and a book about dishwashing, which Simonson gave him a hard time over because Miller cooked at their old restaurant gig while Simonson did the dishes by hand.
"At the end of [the construction], Walter realized a second person was needed to work at night. It had been a one-room store. Now, it was a two-room store," Simonson said of his move into bookselling, noting the store was also open until 11 p.m., an hour later than it is now.
